issues.note: Leader and head are plausible confusables; compare notes are optional by house rule.
Director fact appears in compare note and discrimination note, with often versus usually.
High manager is unidiomatic; senior or top manager is the collocation.
Promoted to manager takes no article; right text and reason.
Correctly flags high manager as not a typical collocation.
Examples name no sport; ball club is American too, so no contradiction.
Mainly in baseball is a fair hedged claim; American soccer mostly says coach.
Correction changes two things; note explains only the article, blurring the error.
Bold word named as word is allowed; first part is plain wording.
Right: senior or top manager, not high manager.
Trains misfits the baseball manager the explanation names; coaches do the training.
Plain, accurate definition; vagueness objection is taste.
In charge of someone's business reasonably covers a performer's manager.
Same director fact stated twice with different strength.
Variety contrast belongs in usage note, not explanation, under house rules.
Become a manager is a common, safe collocation; objection is taste.
Same problem: trains overstates the baseball manager's role.
Rule too absolute: became manager, promoted to manager, manager of the bank drop article.
Duplicated director fact, often versus usually.
Right text, right reason: senior or top manager.
Promoted to manager has no article; learner would copy the error.
Boss note repeats the discrimination paragraph's 'the person you work for'.

findings.F1: The director comparison is stated in both the sense 1 compare note and synonym_discrimination, with different strength (often versus usually).
findings.F2: Collocation 'a high manager' is unidiomatic; English says senior manager or top manager.
findings.F3: Example 'promoted to a manager' wrongly adds an article; the idiom is 'promoted to manager'.
findings.F4: Learner-error correction changes both the article and the preposition, but the note explains only the article.
findings.F5: Sense 2 definition says the manager trains the team, which does not fit the baseball use the explanation names.
findings.F6: Sense 2 uses the explanation field for an American-versus-British usage contrast that belongs in usage_note.
findings.F7: Learner-error note 'Use a before the name of a job' is too absolute; the article is dropped for a unique post (became manager, promoted to manager).
findings.F8: The boss synonym note restates the synonym_discrimination text (one fact, one field).
